body.text: Last Thursday, thousands of Timorese walked from Motael church to Santa Cruz cemetery in Dili, as they do every November 12.

In 1991, 16 years into Indonesia’s occupation of Timor-Leste, which began in 1975 and did not end until 1999, the resistance organized a peaceful rally along the same route, two weeks after Indonesian troops killed the young activist Sebastião Gomes. At the cemetery, soldiers opened fire. More than 271 people were killed, and around 250 more were listed as missing. The nation honors them every year, and the anniversary is now known as National Youth Day.

The same occupation left wounds that are harder to speak about. Timorese women, and some men, endured conflict-related sexual violence (CRSV), including rape, sexual slavery, forced pregnancy and other abuses of comparable gravity. Survivors’ advocates describe this abuse as a weapon, used to break the will of women who resisted the occupation.

Timor-Leste’s Commission for Reception, Truth and Reconciliation gathered around 8,000 statements and found that rape had been committed as a crime against humanity. It documented 853 cases but warned that the real number was likely far higher. The perpetrators were overwhelmingly Indonesian, with more than nine in 10 documented cases attributed to Indonesian security forces and their auxiliaries.

Indonesia has gone only part of the way. In 2008, its president accepted that his government and military bore institutional responsibility for the violence of 1999, and expressed regret. But Jakarta ruled out a formal apology, and no Indonesian commander has been successfully prosecuted. Survivors and those who stand with them are still asking for an apology, real reparations and more help, for themselves and for their children.
The work of recognition is not Indonesia’s alone. More than two decades after independence, survivors are still waiting at home for state reparations, formal recognition, and a memorial.

Timor-Leste has worked hard to thank those who gave so much for independence. Veterans’ pensions took up to 64 percent of the social protection budget in 2019, a sign of how deep that gratitude runs. Survivors have also asked to be recognized as contributors to the same struggle. Instead, many live with stigma and ostracism, and their children, born of rape, are often denied schooling and legal papers.
Mane ho Vizaun Foun, the organization that one of us directs, believes that men share responsibility for this silence, and begins by listening.

Survivors and the people beside them have showed what repair can look like. Between 2023 and 2026, Timorese and international organizations, with the Global Survivors Fund, ran a program called Bukae, after the traditional basket Timorese carry on a long journey. It gave interim support to 455 survivors and children born of war in all 13 municipalities. Most chose to repair their homes or start small businesses with $1,250 dollars each, a modest sum that made a real difference. Bukae was always meant to be a first step, and it has now ended.
In the meantime, 17 survivors died, and 25 more died after sharing their stories but before receiving support.

Lasting reparations are a different task. Indonesia carries the greatest responsibility, and survivors are right to keep asking it to act. Yet Timor-Leste did not wait for anyone before thanking its veterans, and both the truth commission in 2005 and the United Nations women’s rights committee in 2015 called on Timor-Leste itself to provide reparations.

The groundwork for this has already been laid. A draft national reparations policy, prepared in February by the Centro Nacional Chega!, the nation’s memory and human rights center, calls reparations a legal and moral responsibility of the state. Last year, the survivors’ network Pirilampu delivered a petition with more than 700 signatures to political leaders.

Then there is memory. A sculpture by one of us, Mother & Child, has stood in St James’s Square in London since 2019. It was commissioned by Justice for Lai Dai Han, a campaign for the children born to Vietnamese women raped by South Korean soldiers during the Vietnam War, known as the Lai Dai Han, and for their mothers – a story much like Timor-Leste’s. Women assaulted in wartime, children born of that violence, and a state that, campaigners say, has yet to recognize or apologize.

A later sculpture, Petrified Survivors, was unveiled in The Hague in 2025 as the world’s first memorial to honor survivors of CRSV across the world. It shows a woman turned to stone, with a child on her back, trapped in vines. Woven among them is a firefly representing Timor-Leste, a symbol chosen by survivors themselves, in partnership with Mane ho Vizaun Foun. Pirilampu takes its name from the Tetun word for firefly, a light that glows in the darkest night.

We urge Parliament to pass a national reparations law, building on the draft already prepared. We urge the nation to recognize survivors as contributors to independence, as it does its veterans. And we urge a permanent memorial at home, so that the firefly, and the memory of every survivor, lives on in Timor-Leste.

President José Ramos-Horta has called the legacy of Santa Cruz a torch of responsibility. We hope that responsibility will reach every survivor of those years, including those whose suffering was never filmed or named. Honoring Santa Cruz means honoring them too.
